correctness.summary: Lcm does not normalize the sign of its inputs and returns a negative value for negative operands. It calls Gcd (which returns a non-negative gcd for normal inputs) but computes `a / g * b` using the original signed a and b, so a single negative argument yields a negative 'lcm'.
correctness.triggeringInput: Lcm.Run(-4, 6) returns -12 instead of 12. (Both int and long overloads.)
correctness.rootCause: `a / g * b` preserves the sign of a*b; with one negative argument the product is negative. LCM is defined as non-negative, so the result is wrong.
correctness.suggestedFix: Take absolute values of a and b before computing, e.g. compute on |a| and |b| (guarding against MinValue), so the returned lcm is always non-negative. If only positive inputs are intended, document that contract.

perf.summary: Lcm recomputes gcd that the caller may already have, and does a/g then *b as two ops where order is already overflow-safe but division dominates.
perf.currentCost: Each Lcm call runs a full Gcd loop (its own chain of divisions) plus one division 'a / g'. When Lcm is used alongside an existing gcd, the gcd is recomputed.
perf.proposedChange: Provide an overload Lcm.Run(long a, long b, long precomputedGcd) that skips the Gcd.Run call, for callers (e.g. CRT-style accumulation) that already hold g. Keep the existing convenience overload.
perf.rationale: Avoids redundant recomputation of gcd (an entire O(log n) division loop) when the caller already knows it. Pure additive API; same result a/g*b.
perf.risk: Additive overload only — existing behavior unchanged. Caller must pass a correct gcd; document it as an unchecked Run-convention method. a/g*b ordering (divide before multiply) is retained to avoid the a*b overflow.
